source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication
finding: Treats clarify-or-commit as a decision-theory problem. The agent asks only if the expected utility gain of a question beats a per-question cost. This is an explicit value-of-information rule built on Raiffa and Schlaifer.
numbers: NetVoI(q) = VoI(q) - c. Ask the best q only if max NetVoI > 0, else commit. Models GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash. Four domains: mixed-stakes 20 Questions, flight preference, ambiguous WebShop, medical diagnosis.
quote: we formalize the clarify-or-commit decision through three contextual factors: Query Ambiguity, Task Risk, Cognitive Load
limits: Answer space limited to closed yes/no or multiple-choice questions. Question set is predefined; question generation not tested. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Direct template for a scaffold gate: price the test, compare to expected gain, stop when net gain is not positive.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication
finding: The VoI controller matched or beat the best hand-tuned baseline without tuning a threshold.
numbers: Matches or exceeds best tuned baselines in 18 of 20 conditions. Up to 1.36 utility points higher in high-cost settings. Mixed 20Q at c=0.01: VoI utility 14.14 vs best confidence-threshold baseline 11.49 (threshold 0.90).
limits: Baselines tuned by grid search over only 9 settings. No seeds or confidence intervals in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A cost-priced gate removes one tuning knob. Price tests; do not use a fixed round count.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication
finding: Cost sweep table (Gemini-2.5-Flash, Mixed 20Q). VoI beats the best baseline at low and mid cost, but loses at one cost level (c=0.10).
numbers: c=0.01: VoI 8.64 vs best baseline 8.30 (confidence 0.9), margin 0.34. c=0.02: 7.72 vs 6.88, margin 0.84. c=0.05: 5.01 vs 3.65 (round-5 baseline), margin 1.36. c=0.10: VoI 1.38 vs 2.28 (confidence 0.5), margin -0.90. c=0.20 row is garbled in the text extraction; not quoted.
limits: Table read from PDF text extraction; the last row is unreliable. The c=0.10 row shows VoI can lose to a tuned baseline.
agent_relevance: The gate is not uniformly better. Keep a fixed-budget fallback and check at each cost level.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication
finding: Fixed-round questioning shows an inverted U in utility: more questions help, then cost overwhelms the gain. The plain prompt 'ask when needed' is inconsistent and below structured methods. The no-question baseline is near zero accuracy on underspecified 20Q.
numbers: Fixed Round curves peak then fall as rounds grow. Adaptive Prompting 'consistently lower than more structured methods'. No Question accuracy near zero for animal and medical 20Q.
limits: Figure values not in the text. The cause (poorly calibrated self-assessed confidence) is the authors' reading, not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Telling a model 'ask if unsure' is not enough. Compute the stop rule in code (fits G5).

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication
finding: The belief inputs to VoI come from the LLM itself and are only partly calibrated. Calibration was fair on animal guessing, worse on medical diagnosis.
numbers: Calibration measured as argmax accuracy vs predicted probability for GPT-4 and Gemini-2.5-Flash on animals, medical and flight tasks.
limits: No ground-truth distribution, so calibration is a proxy. VoI quality is capped by how well the model estimates the likelihood of each answer (the test quality).
agent_relevance: The value of a noisy test depends on its likelihoods. If the model's likelihoods are off, computed VoI is off. Check against real outcomes.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Picks each next question by estimated expected information gain (EIG) from the LLM's own predictive distribution (Rao-Blackwellised, uses logits). Beats prompting and cheaper heuristics on 20 Questions.
numbers: Success rate %, 100 targets per set. Animals GPT-4o: prompt-only 45, split 83, BED-LLM 93, entropy 88. Animals Mistral-Large: 33/85/95/83. Animals Llama-3.1-8B: 8/49/63/54. Celebrities GPT-4o: 45/63/86/64. Things GPT-4o-mini: 26/38/49/37. Average gain 37.4 points over direct prompting.
limits: Questions are multiple choice. Answerer is an LLM, not a human. Full Bayesian update is too costly, so a filter-and-retain heuristic is used.
agent_relevance: Information gain beats 'ask smart questions' prompting. Small models gain most.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Ablations show which parts of the EIG estimate matter. A wrongly estimated EIG can be far worse than plain entropy.
numbers: Animals, GPT-4o-mini: BED-LLM 88, entropy 79, Data-Estimation 64, Implicit Maximization 47, ICL Beliefs 18.
limits: One setting for the ablation. Entropy alone (no likelihood term) is a strong cheap baseline at 79 vs 88.
agent_relevance: Do not ask the model to 'maximise information' implicitly; compute the score in code. Implicit maximisation scored 47.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Preference elicitation test: 200 simulated user profiles, 5 turns, film recommendations rated 1-5 by an LLM judge. BED-LLM beat prompt-only and entropy, most when questioner and answerer are different model classes.
numbers: 200 profiles, 5 turns, 10 recommendations per turn. Exact scores not in the text I read.
limits: Simulated users and LLM judge. Gains differ with the mismatch between questioner and answerer, which suggests a same-model simulated answerer may share the questioner's biases.
agent_relevance: Same-model simulation of test results may overstate value. Use a different or real answerer when estimating test quality.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT simulates answer branches, scores each question by an information-gain reward, and propagates expected reward up a tree. It raises task success over direct prompting.
numbers: Average +38.1% success rate over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs. Llama3-70B +46.6%. Beats CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, Original-ToT by 28.3%, Adapted-ToT by 12.4%.
limits: Simplified benchmarks: each answer fully eliminates candidates; closed-set setting gives the model the list of outcomes. GPT-4 plays the environment (checked on 10% of logs). Few repeat runs due to API quota.
agent_relevance: An information-gain reward beats a generic self-evaluation reward. Simulation depth capped at 3 for cost.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Per-task results with GPT-4, closed set: medical diagnosis (DX) 97.0% success; MedDG 88.0% with GPT-4 and 81.4% with Gemini1.5-Pro; troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3%.
numbers: DX: UoT mean conversation length in successes 2.0 vs 3.5 and 3.0 for direct-prompt methods. Troubleshooting best MSC 7.8.
limits: Top numbers are closed-set; open-set is lower. Chain-of-Thought and Planning Prompting scored below plain GPT-4 in closed-set 20Q.
agent_relevance: Reasoning prompts without an uncertainty reward can hurt question quality.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Swapping ToT's self-evaluation reward for an uncertainty-based reward lifts ToT; removing the uncertainty reward from UoT lowers it.
numbers: ToT (+UR) gains an average 5.9% over ToT with self-evaluation (GPT-4).
limits: Ablation on one model. t-tests on three runs per dataset for GPT-4 and Llama 3 (Appendix H): few runs.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: a coded information score beats the model's own judgement of a question.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Enhancing LLMs with Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: LLaMA-2-chat-7B asks low-EIG questions in 20 Questions (about 0.3 per question vs 1.0 for a perfect half split). DPO on 55,000 pairs of EIG=1 vs EIG<0.8 questions raises EIG and success.
numbers: Table 1 (8 candidates): zero-shot EIG 0.34, 0.29, 0.35 across three sets; DPO EIG 0.45, 0.40, 0.47. One set: success 56.7% zero-shot, 46.6% fine-tuned, 68.9% DPO; questions per success 7.1 vs 5.2. INLG16: success +12.2 points.
limits: One 7B model plays all roles. On BigBench (29 candidates) success rose but EIG did not (0.31 to 0.28). Abstract targets stay hard: 7.7% to 23.1%.
agent_relevance: Open models are poor at choosing tests that split hypotheses. Gains may not transfer to larger candidate sets.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Enhancing LLMs with Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: Zero-shot model asks more constraint-seeking questions that are less informative; DPO improves them. Zero-shot questions are weak after a 'no' answer; DPO questions zoom in on the identified category.
numbers: Concrete targets +12.5 points and abstract targets +15.4 points with DPO. One set: constraint-seeking share/EIG 47.45%/0.25 zero-shot vs 60.05%/0.33 DPO (Table 3, row assignment not fully verified).
limits: Candidates treated as equally likely. EIG uses yes/no labels from the same LLM; some questions are hard to label (e.g. 'Is it living?' for dinosaur).
agent_relevance: Models underuse negative answers. A rule that updates on a 'no' should be in code.

source: Ding, Tomlin, Durrett (2026) Calibrate-Then-Act: Cost-Aware Exploration in LLM Agents
finding: Pandora's Box test, the closest direct test of 'is a test worth its cost'. Models do not weigh cost against uncertainty alone, but do so near-optimally if told the prior and allowed to think.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, 100 examples, K=3 boxes. Oracle reward 0.649. Prompted non-think: optimal match 11%, reward 0.441. Prompted thinking: 23%, 0.476. Prior given, non-think: 20%, 0.436. Prior given, thinking (CTA): 94% match, reward 0.625.
limits: One small model, toy task. Priors alone did nothing without thinking mode.
agent_relevance: Give the agent numeric priors and costs and let it compute. Without numbers it does not reason about value of information.

source: Ding, Tomlin, Durrett (2026) Calibrate-Then-Act: Cost-Aware Exploration in LLM Agents
finding: Retrieval-augmented QA: always retrieving costs too much; never retrieving is inaccurate. Giving the model an estimate of how likely it is to know the answer gives the best reward, by a small margin.
numbers: Reward: never retrieve 0.226, always retrieve 0.213, prompted non-think 0.244 (retrieves 97.7%), prompted thinking 0.283 (61.4%), CTA 0.293 (65.3%). Accuracy: 22.6%, 57.8%, 61.9%, 50.1%, 51.2%.
limits: CTA edge over prompted thinking is 0.01 reward. Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Fixed always-test or never-test policies lose to an adaptive rule, but the edge can be small.

source: Ding, Tomlin, Durrett (2026) Calibrate-Then-Act: Cost-Aware Exploration in LLM Agents
finding: File-reading coding task: RL-trained agents collapse to always test first; a prior-conditioned agent adapts to the cost ratio. Imperfect priors still help, with smooth decay.
numbers: Mean reward: prompted 0.229, CTA-prompted 0.240, RL 0.259, CTA-RL 0.268. RL agents show 0% code-first traces. Prior-quality sweep (reward at first cost setting): BERT prior (67% acc) 0.382; noisy (52%) 0.365; uniform (46%) 0.349; adversarial (33%) 0.299 (table column assignment partly inferred from text extraction).
limits: Task accuracy is 94 to 99%, so reward differences come from cost, not correctness. An adversarial prior still costs reward.
agent_relevance: A bad estimate of test quality hurts gradually; rough priors still help. Approximate VoI is usable.

source: Piatrashyn et al. (2026) ReDAct: Uncertainty-Aware Deferral for LLM Agents
finding: A cheap model defers a step to an expensive model when its own uncertainty is high. Model uncertainty acts as a noisy test of whether a step is wrong.
numbers: Deferring about 15% of decisions to the large model matches large-model quality on ALFWorld and MiniGrid. Models 70B to 480B (Qwen3-80B, Llama3.3-70B, GPT-5.2, Qwen3-480B). Beats random deferral in every combination.
limits: Step correctness labels come from a GPT-5.2 judge. One exception to the Pareto front (Llama4-Maverick on MiniGrid). Reasoning-level uncertainty discriminated poorly.
agent_relevance: Action-level uncertainty (perplexity, sequence probability, token entropy) is a usable cheap test; uncertainty over free-form reasoning is not.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: Question-Asking LLMs and a Benchmark for Reliable Interactive Clinical Reasoning
finding: Prompting strong LLMs to simply ask follow-up questions made them worse than using the limited information alone. Most samples drew no question at all.
numbers: Basic interactive prompt gave an average 11.3% relative accuracy drop vs same limited information with no questions (Llama-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; MedQA and CRAFT-MD). For most samples no model asked any question.
limits: Simulated patient system. Drop is relative and averaged over models.
agent_relevance: Models are trained to answer, not to seek. Forcing a question should be done by code when it pays (G1: on a signal).

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: Question-Asking LLMs and a Benchmark for Reliable Interactive Clinical Reasoning
finding: An abstention module (confidence by rationale generation and self-consistency) to decide when to ask raised accuracy but did not reach the full-information level.
numbers: Improvement 22.3% from abstention strategies; 10.3% gap remains to the complete-information upper bound; best Scale+RG+SC closes only 51.2% of the gap between Initial and Full information.
limits: Confidence is itself a noisy test. Question relevance matters; filtering irrelevant context helps.
agent_relevance: Deciding when to ask by calibrated confidence helps, yet about half of the lost information is still not recovered.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Frames clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design: sample candidate solutions, generate questions, pick the highest expected information gain over solutions. Reasoning over solutions beats reasoning over question space.
numbers: 20 Questions (animals; 15 ground-truth animals, 5 run seeds, 25 evaluation seeds; GPT-4o-mini answerer) and code generation on HumanEval and APPS (48 non-trivial tasks; zero-shot APPS accuracy 35% vs 70% on HumanEval for GPT-4o-mini). EIG strategies beat implicit and implicit-ToT strategies; 4 requirements elicited.
limits: EIG estimated from logprobs underperformed. For more capable models the gap between baseline and EIG shrinks. EIG needs more LLM calls. Open questions cost the human more effort.
agent_relevance: Choosing questions by expected information over sampled hypotheses is cheap and works, but the gain shrinks as the base model gets stronger.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not update beliefs like a Bayesian across rounds (flight recommendation). Fine-tuning on a Bayesian Assistant's predictions fixes much of it and transfers to new tasks.
numbers: Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5 (7B to 70B). Bayesian-tuned predictions agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time. Human-user check: flight original LLM 37.0% (CI 30.6 to 43.5), Bayesian LLM +38.5 points; hotel 36.7%, +29.4; web shopping 54.0%, +18.6. 720 Prolific participants as assistants; 500 as users.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, not a scaffold. Human choices are inconsistent with stated preferences, so ceilings are lower.
agent_relevance: The posterior update that VoI needs is where models fail. Do the update in code, not in the model.

source: Li et al. (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: Preregistered human study of LM-driven elicitation (open questions, yes/no questions, edge cases) vs user-written prompts and labels. Elicited responses were often more informative and took less mental effort.
numbers: 388 Prolific participants, 6 elicitation methods x 3 domains (content recommendation, moral reasoning, email validation), 20 to 30 per cell.
limits: Better only 'sometimes'. In email validation, user-written prompts slightly lowered performance vs no elicitation. Simulated personas did not always match human results.
agent_relevance: Real answerers are noisy and sometimes wrong about their own preferences. Treat the answer channel as uncertain.

source: Andukuri et al. (2024) STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
finding: A self-taught reasoner trained to ask questions that raise the probability of the gold answer. Its responses beat the initial model's.
numbers: Win rate 72% after two iterations vs initial model; 65% with a different roleplayer; 62% peak with gemma-7b roleplayer. One ablation drifted back to 50% by iteration three.
limits: Win rates judged by GPT-4. The gold-response variant reverted to 50% due to hallucination. Trained, not scaffolded.
agent_relevance: Training for question quality can work but is fragile across iterations.

source: Liu et al. (2025) CostBench: Evaluating Multi-Turn Cost-Optimal Planning and Adaptation for LLM Tool-Use Agents
finding: Cost-aware tool choice is weak even in frontier models. Exact match to the cost-optimal tool sequence drops with length and with dynamic cost changes.
numbers: Ten LLMs. GPT-5 near perfect at length 5, about 75% at length 8; other models below 60% at length 5. Performance falls about 40% under dynamic conditions. A cost change drops GPT-5 exact match by about 20 points.
limits: Travel-planning domain only; exact match, not utility.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an agent to price its own tool calls. Give costs and compare in code.

source: Raiffa and Schlaifer (1961) Applied Statistical Decision Theory
finding: Founding text. Defines the expected value of sample information (EVSI), bounded above by the expected value of perfect information (EVPI). Cited as the origin of VoI by Dong et al. 2026 (opened, c01).
numbers: not extracted this session
limits: Not opened. Claim rests on the citation in c01 and the standard definition. No numbers.
agent_relevance: Ceiling rule: no test is worth more than perfect information. Use as a stop rule.

source: Howard (1966) Information Value Theory
finding: Cited by Dong et al. 2026 as the second root of value of information in decision analysis.
numbers: not extracted this session
limits: Not opened; only the citation in c01 seen.
agent_relevance: Same as c01.

source: Heckerman, Horvitz, Nathwani (1992) Toward normative expert systems: Pathfinder
finding: Older AI system for lymph-node pathology using influence diagrams and value of information to choose the next test. Recalled from background knowledge, not verified this session.
numbers: not extracted this session
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Shows VoI inside an expert-system loop decades before LLM agents.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2023) ChatGPT's information seeking strategy: insights from the 20-Questions game
finding: Cited by Mazzaccara et al. 2024 and UoT (both opened) as showing ChatGPT's 20-Questions questions are low in informativeness with limited success.
numbers: not extracted this session
limits: Not opened; claim taken from citing papers. No numbers.
agent_relevance: Baseline evidence that plain prompting asks poor questions.
